claims.feature: antiquarian verbs on the title page
claims.claim: The Red Book's title-page vocabulary of 'compiled', 'observations', 'accounts' and 'translated' gives it the antiquarian air of Percy's Reliques, Macpherson's translations and Chatterton's Antiquities.
claims.source: Will Sherwood, 'Tolkien and the Age of Forgery', JTR 11.1 (2020)

claims.claim: The Red Book's history of interwoven, identifiable source-traditions and voices produces the effect of age and lends the text antiquarian authenticity.
claims.source: Will Sherwood, 'Tolkien and the Age of Forgery', JTR 11.1 (2020), citing Painter 2016

claims.claim: The antiquarian forger's toolkit that Groom lists for Chatterton (calligraphy, manuscripts, maps, heraldry, prefaces, footnotes, appendices, glossaries) is the same kit Tolkien uses to immerse readers in Arda.
claims.source: Will Sherwood, 'Tolkien and the Age of Forgery', JTR 11.1 (2020), citing Groom 2014

claims.claim: Richard C. West calls the Red Book a spurious source whose authority appeals not to the old and familiar but to the modern mystique of scholarly research.
claims.quote: the modern mystique of scholarly research

claims.claim: Kristin Thompson identifies the Red Book as a found-manuscript conceit in the line running back to Samuel Richardson's eighteenth-century novels.

Flieger describes The Lord of the Rings as presented at four levels at once: the story itself, a version referencing other versions, a historical artifact (the Red Book), and a modern edition complete with scholarly and critical apparatus.
claims.quote: complete with scholarly and critical apparatus

claims.claim: Tolkien went to elaborate lengths to construct a credible book tradition, with repeated mentions of Bilbo's diary, his Translations from the Elvish, and masses of notes in his room at Rivendell.

Flieger finds The Hobbit's frame rather fragile because its narrator often speaks in a voice that cannot be Bilbo's, whereas The Lord of the Rings has the frame carefully embedded from the earliest drafts.
claims.page: § The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Appendix A's Kings of the Mark section uses annalistic headings, dates recording great events, and later editor's footnotes (such as identifying Holdwine as Meriadoc), giving the look of authentic historical documentation.

Brljak argues that the pseudo-editorial, pseudo-philological and pseudo-translational framework is both the cornerstone and crowning achievement of Tolkien's mature literary work, modelled on the impression of depth he admired in Beowulf.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editorial framing of The Lord of the Rings'

claims.claim: Turner notes the frame works at two levels at once, treating the world of the story as historical fact while creating for the reader the illusion of a direct link through time and space.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editorial framing of The Lord of the Rings' (citing Turner)
claims.quote: the world of the story as historical fact

claims.claim: Pezzini argues the meta-textual frame lets Tolkien write in contrasting styles, alternating between high and low, and to dignify the humble while writing in the low style.
claims.source: Bradley Birzer, 'How Did Tolkien Write Great Books?' (Law & Liberty, reviewing Pezzini)
claims.quote: alternating between high and low, transcendent and earthy

claims.claim: Pezzini describes the Red Book as an authorial mosaic (Bilbo, Frodo, Sam as last hand) stitched into the narration by 'remembering formulas' such as 'Pippin afterwards recalled little' and by reportorial scenes where separated hobbits recount what they witnessed.
claims.source: Erik Jampa Andersson, 'The Red Book: Giuseppe Pezzini on Tolkien's Meta-Textual Frame' (Substack, lecture notes)

claims.claim: The translator persona of Appendix F would rather change the English language and coin new words than deliver a substandard translation, so consistency of rendering governs the whole record.
claims.source: N. Lurquin, 'Translating the Red Book of Westmarch' (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern blog)
claims.quote: rather change the English language and make new words

claims.claim: Groom places Tolkien in the English antiquarian line of Swift, Chatterton and Stukeley as one who enlists the aesthetics of antiquarianism, and Sherwood reads the non-narrative elements as Tolkien improving on antiquarian forgery to create modern fantasy's conventions.
claims.page: § Tolkien in the English antiquarian tradition

verdicts.trueWording: the antiquarian air of Percy's Reliques, Macpherson's translations and Chatterton's 'Antiquities'
verdicts.note: Raw PDF reached via Wayback id_ capture (live viewcontent.cgi returned HTTP 403 Cloudflare). Journal p.23 exactly as cited: "Words like 'compiled', 'observations', 'accounts' and 'translated' give The Red Book of Westmarch the antiquarian air of Percy's Reliques, Macpherson's translations and Chatterton's 'Antiquities', placing it strongly in the antiquarian tradition". Every limb (the four words, and all three antiquarian comparanda) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: produce the effect of age' and crucially lend the text antiquarian authenticity
verdicts.note: Journal p.24 (confirmed by the page footer), as cited. Full sentence: "Its history of 'interwoven multivalent, identifiable source-traditions . . . and voices [therefore] produce the effect of age' and crucially lend the text antiquarian authenticity (Painter, 2016, p. 125)." The Painter 2016 attribution in the claim's source field is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: loaded his pseudo-antique writings with prefaces, footnotes, appendices, and glossaries
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim inside the Groom 2014 p.295 quotation: Chatterton crafted 'calligraphy; produced his own complex medieval manuscripts, maps, sketches, and heraldry; loaded his pseudo-antique writings with prefaces, footnotes, appendices, and glossaries'; the next sentence supplies the Tolkien limb: "To a reader of Tolkien these will all sound familiar as they are the techniques that are used to immerse readers into Arda." Metadata nit only, not a claim limb: the passage sits on journal p.19 (PDF p.21), not p.18 as the page field says.

verdicts.trueWording: an appeal not to the old and familiar, but to the modern mystique of scholarly research
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext (action=raw), § Analysis, as cited. "In the Tolkien scholar Richard C. West's view, Tolkien's Red Book is a pastiche of scholarship. It functions, he writes, as what scholars would call a spurious source, but the authority it imparts is by an appeal not to the old and familiar, but to the modern mystique of scholarly research." Both limbs (spurious source; the mystique appeal) present.

verdicts.trueWording: used in English literature since Samuel Richardson's novels Pamela (1740) and Clarissa
verdicts.note: § Analysis: 'The "found manuscript conceit",[Thompson 1988] employed by Tolkien to situate The Hobbit as a part of The Red Book of Westmarch, has been used in English literature since Samuel Richardson's novels Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded (1740) and Clarissa (1747-1748)'. The Kristin Thompson attribution is carried by the ref (cite journal, last=Thompson first=Kristin, Mythlore 1988) rather than in prose; a gallery caption repeats it: 'Tolkien was following the tradition of Samuel Richardson's 1740 novel Pamela ... in the conceit of a found manuscript.'

verdicts.trueWording: as a modern edition of that book complete with scholarly and critical apparatus
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext. "Flieger states that Tolkien presents The Lord of the Rings at four levels: 'as the story itself; as one version of that story embodying references to other versions; as a historical artifact - the Red Book; [and] as a modern edition of that book complete with scholarly and critical apparatus'." All four levels present verbatim. Metadata nit only: the passage is in § Book > Summary describing Part 1 of Flieger's book, not '§ Part 2' as the page field says.

verdicts.trueWording: went to 'elaborate lengths' ... Bilbo's 'diary' and 'Translations from the Elvish'
verdicts.note: § Red Book of Westmarch, as cited. "Verlyn Flieger writes that Tolkien, seeking to present his Middle-earth writings as a credible mythology, needed to create a 'credible book tradition'. He went to 'elaborate lengths' to achieve this, including many mentions of Bilbo's 'diary' and 'Translations from the Elvish' ... complete with 'the masses of notes and paper in his room at Rivendell'." Every limb of the claim is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: rather fragile, since the book's narrator often speaks in a voice that cannot be Bilbo's
verdicts.note: "Flieger notes that The Hobbit's frame story is rather fragile, since the book's narrator often speaks in a voice that cannot be Bilbo's. In The Lord of the Rings, on the other hand, Tolkien carefully embedded the frame story in the text, from the earliest drafts." Both halves of the contrast supported. The passage sits in the sub-section § Red Book of Westmarch, under the top-level section named in the page field.

verdicts.trueWording: the Holdwine=Meriadoc identification is labelled 'Scribal gloss', not 'Later editor's footnote'
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the parenthetical example - the page assigns 'Later editor's footnote' to the footnote about Eowyn's shield-arm, and labels the bracketed '[This Holdwine was none other than Meriadoc the Magnificent who was Master of Buckland.]' a 'Scribal gloss', a distinct third category
verdicts.note: § Paratexts table (Croft 2018) supports the rest: the row labels are 'Annalistic heading', 'Annalistic dates and text recording great events of the past', 'Later editor's footnote' and 'Scribal gloss', over Appendix A. II 'The House of Eorl', The Kings of the Mark, Third Line. The 'look of authentic historical documentation' limb is supported in other words - the paratexts 'resonat[e]' or 'collaborat[e]' with the main text 'making it more believable', under the table caption 'Tolkien's representation of historical editing of ancient documents'. The claim's quote field is empty, so the grade turns wholly on the limbs.

verdicts.trueWording: is both the cornerstone and crowning achievement of Tolkien's mature literary work
verdicts.note: § An external editorial frame: "Brljak argues that this framework 'is both the cornerstone and crowning achievement of Tolkien's mature literary work', and that the pseudo-editorial, pseudo-philological, and pseudo-translational apparatus contributes greatly to the effect." The Beowulf limb is supported immediately before: Brljak notes Tolkien's praise of Beowulf and Shippey's 'virtual identity of motive and of technique', an affinity that 'extended to creating an impression of depth', 'unattainable vistas', 'an echo of an echo', by 'an intricate metafictional structure'. Quote string verbatim (with the Oxford comma, as the quote field has it).

verdicts.trueWording: elements of the frame story function at multiple levels
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the count 'two levels at once' - the page (and its section heading) says 'multiple levels', never two
verdicts.note: § Multiple levels: "The scholar of literature Allan Turner comments that elements of the frame story function at multiple levels; in particular, metatextual elements like the appendices '[treat] the world of the story as historical fact, at the same time [creating] for the reader the illusion of a direct link through time and space with his/her own world through the persona of the \"editor\"'." The quote is verbatim and the two substantive halves (historical fact; illusion of a direct link through time and space) are both supported; only the numeral is the page's 'multiple', and the claim also drops the closing qualifier 'with his/her own world through the persona of the editor'.

verdicts.trueWording: given permission to write in contrasting styles, alternating between high and low, transcendent and earthy
verdicts.note: Live page fetched with a browser UA, HTTP 200. "By claiming different authors, Tolkien, then, is given permission to write in contrasting styles, alternating between high and low, transcendent and earthy. Further, while writing in the latter style, Tolkien can dignify the humble." 'the latter style' is the earthy/low one, so the dignify-the-humble limb holds. Attribution limb holds in context: the sentence stands in Birzer's review of Pezzini, directly after 'Pezzini convincingly argues that...', and the review quotes Pezzini on 'the meta-textual frame' twice; note the page's own phrasing for the mechanism is 'By claiming different authors' rather than 'the meta-textual frame'.

verdicts.trueWording: what Giuseppe calls the 'remembering' formulas ... the 'authorial mosaic'
verdicts.note: Live Substack page, HTTP 200. Every limb present: "There are, first, what Giuseppe calls the 'remembering' formulas: like when ... we are told that 'Pippin afterwards recalled little of either food or drink' (95)"; Sam is "the last hand to join what Giuseppe refers to as the 'authorial mosaic' of The Lord of the Rings"; Bilbo is 'The First Author', Frodo 'The Second Author', Sam 'The Third Author'; and the reportorial limb: "the more direct 'reporting' moments, i.e. occasions when the hobbits, having been split up, come back together and recount what happened." Only nit: the page says the mosaic 'of The Lord of the Rings', the claim says 'the Red Book' - the same object inside the frame, and the page opens by identifying the Red Book as the source material.

verdicts.trueWording: his forward in the first edition of The Fellowship of the Ring
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'the translator persona of Appendix F' - the post grounds the translator conceit in Tolkien's foreword to the first edition of The Fellowship of the Ring and never mentions Appendix F (zero occurrences on the page)
verdicts.note: Live blogspot page, HTTP 200. The quoted limb is verbatim: 'He would rather change the English language and make new words than provide us with a substandard translation.' The consistency limb is supported in other words: 'He created words in the English language simply so he could consistently translate the Red Book of Westmarch from Westron into English.' Only the Appendix F locus fails; the post's stated source is 'his forward in the first edition of The Fellowship of the Ring'.

Raw wikitext. The quote is NOT word for word - the page reads Groom notes that Tolkien was not a 'literary forger' like Chatterton, but that his facsimile pages of the Book of Mazarbul 'enlist[ed] the aesthetics of antiquarianism' and that he 'adopts the techniques of literary forgery' - bracketed past tense, and predicated of the Book of Mazarbul facsimile rather than of Tolkien at large, hence SUBSTANCE not VERBATIM. Both other limbs hold: 'Nick Groom, in A Companion to J. R. R. Tolkien, places Tolkien in the tradition of English antiquarianism', with Swift, Stukeley, Chatterton (plus Percy and Blake) as the line, tabulated as 'Nick Groom's analysis of Tolkien's relationship to English antiquarianism'; and 'Sherwood argues that Tolkien intentionally set about improving on antiquarian forgery, eventually creating \"the codes and conventions of modern fantasy literature\"', with Sherwood quoted on the non-narrative elements that 'will all sound familiar as they are the techniques that [Tolkien] used to immerse readers into Arda'. Metadata nit: the 'enlist[ed]' sentence is in § Antiquarian elements in Tolkien's writings > Artwork, not § Tolkien in the English antiquarian tradition.
